name: Xanthine Orange
lede: Xanthine Orange is a deep burnt orange first plated by Ridgway in 1912, a color that plays an accent far more often than any other role in the paintings where our archive finds it.

sections.title: A deep orange, and a Japanese echo
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 atlas plates this color at plate III, hue 13, tone i, a scan of an aged plate treated here as approximate [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS circular later classed it as deep orange, 5.4 units from its own block center, and the Munsell notation is 3.7YR 5.5/11.6 [1]. Our sources do not explain where the English word "xanthine" was coined as a color name; the books consulted leave its origin undocumented beyond its classification here as a mineral or pigment word [1].

Our library cross-references two Japanese traditional names at nearly this hue: Kincha (金茶), meaning golden brown, and Kohaku-iro (琥珀色), meaning amber color [1]. The closest named color on screen is [[browny-orange]], 3.0 units away and described as almost the same; [[alloy-orange]] follows at 3.9, read as darker, [[ochre]] at 4.0, also almost the same, and [[rust-orange]] at 4.6 [3]. Our graph also finds a gem twin: a flame-orange [[gem:spinel|spinel]] sits only 2.9 units from this hue [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this orange in 0.51 percent of 23,781 paintings, 121 of them, and the within-painting lens isolates it as a dominant area in 120 of those, nearly every one, as photographed [2]. That ranks it ahead of 62 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 13 of 1,674 paintings, present in 0.8 percent of the 1,674 paintings (13 of them) dated to that century, 1.4 times its museums' baseline rate [2].

Inside a painting it plays an accent 84 percent of the time, the highest accent rate of any color, by lightness rank rather than by eye [2]. It is strongly over-represented in Indian painting, 3.9 times the expected rate, and further still in the Mughal and Pahari movements specifically, 6.5 and 6.4 times their baselines [2]. The earliest match in our archive is a painting dated to 1250, 662 years before Ridgway's 1912 record of the name; that gap marks a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not the pigment itself, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. In printed English the word rose fastest in the 1910s and peaked in the 1930s (Google Books, all senses of the word) [2].
